---
title: "Limitations"
---

Some of these follow from PHP itself and will not change. Others are milestone
boundaries and will. Each one says which.

## A cell cannot redeclare a class or a function

PHP has no way to replace a class, interface, trait, enum, or function once it
is declared, so re-running a cell that declares one cannot work. The kernel
refuses such a cell before executing anything, naming the collision:

```
RedeclarationError: The class, interface, trait or enum "Widget" was already
declared in this session, and PHP cannot redeclare it. Restart the kernel to
redefine it.
```

Refusing is deliberate. Letting it reach `eval()` would be an uncatchable fatal
error that ends the kernel rather than an error the notebook can show.

The session records a name only once PHP really holds it, so a cell that failed
to declare anything leaves the name free. `class Widget extends Typo {}` throws
and declares nothing, and the corrected cell runs. The common case this serves
is running cells out of order: define a base class after its subclass, run the
subclass cell first, then run them in the right order, and it works.

A conditional declaration is not affected, because PHP does not bind one at
compile time:

```php
if (! function_exists('helper')) {
    function helper() { /* ... */ }
}
```

This follows from PHP and will not change.

## A cell cannot declare a namespace

A `namespace` declaration is refused. Changing namespace part way through a
session breaks name resolution for everything already defined, and the kernel
would have no honest way to decide which namespace a later cell belongs to.
Use fully qualified names, or `use` statements, which do carry from one cell to
the next.

This is a deliberate refusal and is not planned to change.

## Every cell runs under strict types

The kernel prepends `declare(strict_types=1);` to each cell, because PHP accepts
that declaration nowhere but the first statement. A cell writing it for itself is
fine and the kernel removes the duplicate. `declare(strict_types=0)` is refused,
since the kernel cannot honor it, and so is `declare(encoding=...)`, which has
the same first-statement rule. `declare(ticks=...)` is left alone.

## References and `$this` do not survive between cells

Variables are carried across cells by value. A reference taken in one cell is an
ordinary copy in the next, and `$this` has no meaning at a notebook's top level.
Objects, arrays, scalars, and resources all persist normally. Every PHP REPL
behaves this way.

## A closure called from another cell has no line in its traceback

A traceback names the cell and the line for ordinary functions and methods,
across cells:

```
RuntimeException: from the function
  at Cell 1, line 3, in boom()
  at Cell 2, line 2
```

A closure is different. PHP's trace does not say where a closure was declared,
and every cell's `eval()` shares one file name, so a closure declared in one
cell and called from another cannot be placed. The kernel reports the frame
without a location rather than guessing:

```
LogicException: from the closure
  in a closure
  at Cell 4, line 4
```

Naming a line it could not know would send you to the wrong place, which is
worse than naming none. The call site is still reported. This is a milestone
boundary.

## A cell whose value is null shows no output

`var_dump($x);`, `Juphyter\display($df)`, and any other call that returns
nothing produce no `Out[N]`, the same way a Python notebook shows nothing for
`None`. Every other value is shown, including `0`, `false`, `''`, `[]`, and
`'null'`.

## A cell that calls `exit` or `die` ends the kernel

PHP cannot catch either, so the process goes. The kernel reports it rather than
disappearing silently:

```
SystemExit: The cell ended the kernel process with exit or die, so nothing
further can run. Restart the kernel to carry on.
```

Anything the cell printed first is still shown. This follows from PHP.

## Interrupting needs pcntl, and a cell can still swallow it

The stop button sends a signal, so the PHP binary running cells needs the
`pcntl` extension with its functions callable. `juphyter install` checks the
binary it names and warns when it cannot signal, including the case where the
extension is loaded but its functions sit in `disable_functions`.

An interrupt arrives as `Juphyter\Engine\Interrupt`, which extends `Error`
rather than `Exception` so that ordinary defensive code does not absorb it. A
cell that catches `Throwable` in a loop can still swallow it, which is the same
trade Python makes by putting `KeyboardInterrupt` outside `Exception`.

## A frame's numbers in an HTML table are not pillar's

A frame's `text/plain` output is phibble's own, character for character. The
HTML table is the kernel's, and it formats a float with PHP's own string
conversion rather than reproducing pillar's significant-figure logic, so a wide
`dbl` column can read differently in the two. The HTML header also omits the
group count that the text output carries. Both are milestone boundaries.

## macOS and Linux only

The kernel interrupts a cell with POSIX signals and reaps a child process, which
the Windows PHP build does not support. This matches the platforms the phit and
phpolars extensions declare.

## Not yet implemented

These are milestone boundaries with nothing in the design against them:

- **Documentation on hover.** Jupyter's `inspect_request` is not answered, so
  shift-tab shows nothing.
- **Reading input.** A cell cannot prompt, so `readline()` and `fgets(STDIN)`
  have nothing to read.
- **Magics.** There are no `%`-prefixed commands.
- **Widgets.** `ipywidgets` is not supported.
- **The debugger.** Jupyter's debug protocol is not implemented, so JupyterLab's
  debugger does not attach.
- **A Vega-Lite 6 renderer.** phiz emits Vega-Lite 6 and JupyterLab's bundled
  renderer reads version 5, so plots are published under the version 5 MIME
  type. Everything phiz currently produces compiles under the renderer
  JupyterLab ships, and the static SVG covers anything that does not.
